author: Ryan Burge
title: Who Do Teenagers Turn To When They Doubt Their Religion?
summary: Gen Alpha Christians have parents, grandparents, and pastors. Four in ten non-religious teens have no one.
full_content:
What does the future of faith look like?

That’s a question I get asked all the time by folks who are interested in what’s just over the horizon when it comes to American religion. Often that’s motivated by a desire to see if there’s a religious revival right around the corner or maybe the idea that faith is just changing in its conception and expression for the next generation.

It’s actually not an easy question to answer for a very practical reason – it’s very difficult to actually do a survey of teenagers in the United States. For lots of ethical and legal reasons almost every survey of American religion deals only with adults, that is, only those who are at least 18 years old. Which certainly gives us a glimpse of the future but just a partial one.

But now I have an opportunity (thanks to the Fuller Youth Institute) to do a deep dive into the spiritual and religious lives of Generation Alpha. They conducted a survey of nearly 3,000 13-17 year olds in the middle of 2025 that asked all kinds of nuanced questions about their faith, their doubts and their relationships. The folks at Fuller have written a lengthy research report about this that you can access from this link, but then I partnered with them to do my own exploration into the data and present some of the results to readers of this newsletter.

I wanted to focus on just a small handful of questions that I think offer a bit of unique insight into how teenagers are dealing with their doubts about the existential questions in life and how relationships play a really interesting role in helping Gen Alpha navigate some of their struggles.

Let me just start by showing you the share of 13 to 17 year olds who said that they experienced doubt “most of the time” or “almost always” in six different areas.

The group that said that they experienced the least amount of doubt across nearly all items was Christian teenagers. Among Christians, only 15% said that they “felt unsure whether God or a higher power is real” most of the time or always. That was 9 points lower than those of non-Christian faiths, and 20 points lower than teenagers who said that they were spiritual but not religious. Christian teens were also half as likely to say that they “felt frustrated or upset with God” compared to their peers.

There were several areas in which Christian and non-religious teens had similar responses, though. For instance, 16-18% of each group said that they “questioned my religious or spiritual beliefs” frequently. One potential reason for that is that lots of nones just weren’t thinking about their religious beliefs at all. The same explanation could be used for the question about feeling confused about faith or spirituality, too.

I do need to point out that the SBNR (spiritual but not religious) teenagers always scored near the top of the doubting scale for each of these six statements, though. They seem to be stuck in the middle of the faith spectrum while their church and non-religious peers are at the two ends of the spectrum.

I wanted to zoom in a bit on those Christian members of Gen Alpha, though, in order to show you which of these statements seemed to elicit the most doubts and which ones were not really a struggle for 13-17 year old Christians.

The area in which Gen Alpha Christians clearly struggle the most is answering that age-old question, “Why do bad things happen?” About a third of these Christians said that this was something that they pondered most of the time or almost always. That was followed by feeling disconnected from God or their own faith. However, I do need to point out that just 8% of Gen Alpha Christians said that they struggled with this thought on a near-constant basis.

The bottom of the list was interesting to me, too. The idea that Gen Alpha Christians aren’t sure of God’s existence is refuted strongly by this data. In this group, 43% said that this was never a doubt that they had and another 24% said it only popped up in their mind every once in a while. That means that two-thirds of young Christians are not struggling with the question of God’s existence in any real way. I also need to flag the fact that only about 10% of Gen Alpha Christians said that they were upset with God most of the time.

In general, I don’t get the sense from this data that 13-17 year old Christians are really struggling on a regular basis with some of the biggest questions about faith. Just the opposite, in fact. There was no statement that rose above 15% in the “almost always” category, and most were in the single digits.

But that got me wondering if these young Christians struggled more with doubts the more often they attended religious services.

And the answer to that question is pretty clear from the data – not really. I mean, if you trace each of the bar graphs for each of these six statements, what you find is that oftentimes the confidence intervals overlap in such a way that there’s no statistical difference between those Christians who never attend religious services compared to those who are at church multiple times per week.

It’s interesting to note that a never-attending Christian is just as likely to say that they feel confused about their faith or spirituality compared to a weekly attender. The same is true for feeling unsure about the existence of God, too. Which is worth some reflection around the question of why a teenage Christian who never attends church has the same certainty around God’s existence as their peer who is in church all of the time.

The one area in which there is a clear difference across attendance levels, however, is the question of why bad things happen. For those young Christians who attend never, seldom, or monthly, this is a constant thought for them. In fact, these are the highest percentages in the entire graph (around 37% say this is something on their minds most of the time or always). But as attendance hits that weekly mark, these concerns drop dramatically. Among Christian teens who attend church multiple times per week, it’s just 20%. So this is one area in which we can say attendance has a really clear and large impact on doubts.

So, we’ve established that lots of members of Gen Alpha do struggle with some spiritual and religious beliefs from time to time, but who do they speak to when they are trying to work through some of those issues? There was a question on the survey that asked exactly that and allowed the teenagers to select from a long list of potential conversation partners.

The one selection that was easily the most popular of all was “parents/caregivers.” In the full sample of Gen Alpha, about half of all respondents chose this one. No other group was even close. “Friends” came in second place, but it was only selected by 29% of respondents. Also, a surprising share of Gen Alpha indicated that they spoke with their grandparents on a regular basis about their doubts (19%).

What doesn’t show up on this list a whole lot? Well, very few teenagers are turning to podcasts or books to help them wrestle with their doubts (just 5%). And a vanishingly small number say that they talk to a therapist, a teacher, or a coach when they are going through a difficult time (4% each).

I get the clear impression from this list that family is incredibly important in the lives of Gen Alpha, but I wanted to take this analysis one step further by breaking the sample into Christians vs all others. The graph below is the share of each group that chose any of these options in their top three.

This may be the most interesting graph in this entire article because it paints an entirely different picture of how Christian young people talk through their doubts compared to their non-Christian peers. For instance, a Christian member of Gen Alpha was eight points more likely to put parents/caregivers in their top three compared to the rest of the sample (54% vs 46%). However, when it comes to listing friends, the rest of the sample was eight points more likely to include this group compared to Christians (34% vs 26%).

I don’t want to speculate too much, but I wonder if this discrepancy is due, at least in part, to the fact that Christian teenagers have a more supportive family life. This gains support when looking at the line for grandparents. Among Christian teens, 22% chose this one in their top three compared to just 15% of the rest of the sample.

I did want to direct your attention to the bottom of the graph, too. I see very little evidence that non-Christians are much more likely to seek out support in online spaces or that they will turn to a counselor, a teacher, or a coach compared to Christians.

But there’s one finding that I’ve been intentionally ignoring in the last two graphs that is worth returning to now. It’s the share of Gen Alpha who indicated that they had no one to talk to about their doubts. In the full sample, about one in five teenagers indicated that this was the situation that they were facing in their lives. In the prior graph, you can clearly see a huge divergence on this question, too. Among Christian teenagers, just 11% chose this option. It was 30% among the rest of the sample.

Look what happens when I calculate the response to that question across the five religious traditions in the survey.

Christian members of Gen Alpha are much less likely to say that they have no one to talk to about their doubts compared to the rest of their peers. The gaps between these two groups are incredibly stark. For the SBNRs, 28% said that they had no one to converse with about their doubts. However, it’s the non-religious teenagers who score the highest on this question at 40%.

Now, why would this be the case? One potential explanation is that their parents are non-religious and the teen wouldn’t feel comfortable talking about such matters with them. Another hypothesis is that they just don’t have a strong relationship with their parents, generally speaking.

The faith of a teenager is more than just their personal orientation toward God or the Church. It’s also deeply intertwined with the relationships that they have and the connections that they form. This was certainly true for me as I grew up in the Millennial generation, and it doesn’t seem like much has changed for Gen Alpha, either.

Having doubts is certainly a part of being a teenager. Having someone to discuss those issues with seems important to faith formation. Unfortunately, it seems Christian youth have a huge advantage in this area. In my opinion, that leaves a deficit for everyone else that needs to be reflected on by those who work with young people.

Code for this post can be found here.

Ryan P. Burge is a professor of practice at the Danforth Center on Religion and Politics at Washington University.
rewritten_title: Four in Ten Non-Religious Teens Have No One to Talk To

author: Daniel K. Williams
title: What This Week’s Midterm Elections Revealed about American Christianity and Politics
summary: This week’s midterm election results revealed two realities about contemporary American Christianity and partisanship that could shape American politics in the next election cycle and beyond.
full_content:
This week’s midterm election results revealed two realities about contemporary American Christianity and partisanship that could shape American politics in the next election cycle and beyond.

The first is that the Christian Right is still just as alive and well as it has ever been. White evangelical loyalty to the Republican Party has not diminished. Nor has white evangelical voter turnout.

The second is that although mainline Protestantism is much smaller than evangelicalism, the Democrats can defeat the Religious Right in the Bible belt and the American heartland when they recruit mainline Protestant candidates who make faith a central part of their campaign.

If we understand these two realities, we will be better positioned to understand the current direction of American electoral politics, and we may have a better sense of what both parties’ options are as they prepare for the 2028 presidential election.

1) The Christian Right is still alive and well, and white evangelical voters are still Republican.

Shortly before the election, some pundits noted a softening in evangelical support for Donald Trump. A Pew Research Center survey found that white evangelical approval of Trump dropped by 20 percentage points (from 78 percent to 58 percent) between January 2025 and October 2026.

But when a reporter asked me a week or two ago whether this suggested that evangelicals might be willing to vote for Democrats in the midterms, I said the answer was no, and I pointed to the 2006 election as evidence. In 2004, white evangelicals gave George W. Bush overwhelming support; 78 percent of white evangelical voters cast their ballots for him that year. Yet evangelicals’ approval of Bush eventually declined because of the general disillusionment with the Iraq War. By June 2007, only 44 percent of white evangelicals said they approved of his job performance. Yet that did not make them Democrats. Exit polls showed that between 70 and 72 percent of white evangelical voters voted Republican in the 2006 midterm elections. And in 2008, 73 percent voted Republican in the presidential contest between Barack Obama and John McCain.

2006 was a “blue wave” election, yet white evangelicals remained loyal to the Republican Party. 2008 brought another “blue wave,” yet white evangelicals again mostly voted Republican.

The same was true this year to an even greater extent. Even though the 2026 midterms produced an even bigger blue wave (or even “blue tsunami”) than the 2006 midterms did, white evangelicals remained even more strongly Republican. Eighty-two percent of white evangelical voters voted Republican in congressional elections this year, according to an NBC voter exit poll.

This result is almost identical to previous midterm election polls. In 2022, a CNN exit poll found that 83 percent of white evangelical voters cast their ballots for the Republicans. Seventy-five percent did so in 2018, and 78 percent did so in 2014.

This corresponds well to the general evangelical voting pattern in presidential elections. In the last twenty-five years, white evangelical support for a Republican presidential candidate in the general election has never dropped below 73 percent.

As long as 70-80 percent or more of white evangelical voters continue to perceive the Democratic Party as antithetical to their interests, they will never cast their ballot for the Democrats. They may well become disillusioned with Trump (indeed, nearly apparently already have), but that won’t stop them from supporting the Republican candidate in the next election.

Nor does it seem to stop them from showing up at the polls. White evangelical voters comprised 17 percent of the general electorate this year, according to the NBC exit poll. According to Ryan Burge’s analysis of the 2024 CES survey data, 17 percent of all American adults are white evangelicals. So, while different surveys have slightly different ways of defining and counting evangelicals, an election in which 17 percent of the voters were white evangelicals seems to be on par for a national adult population that is also 17 percent white evangelical.

In short, the white evangelical vote was remarkably stable this year. Despite an unpopular war in Iran, high gas prices, and President Trump’s unpopularity, white evangelicals’ votes were exactly in line with what they were in 2020, 2022, and 2024 – and they were not far off from where they were in the pre-Trump era.

So, unless there is an unprecedented (and completely unanticipated) evangelical realignment in the next two years, I would expect that in 2028, the Republicans will win about 80-83 percent of the white evangelical vote, with about 15-17 percent of white evangelicals voting Democratic. And I would expect that white evangelical voter turnout will continue to be predictably strong – at least in line with other demographic groups.

If the Religious Right is defined by the number of white evangelicals who always vote Republican, it’s still alive and well. This “blue tsunami” election did nothing to change it.

Similarly, the areas of the country that were opposed to abortion before the midterm election continued to express opposition to abortion during the election even as some other regions of the country reaffirmed the legalization of abortion. In Idaho, a referendum to legalize abortion was defeated, which means that the prohibition against abortion in Idaho will stand. And since even the most devout of the Christians running as Democrats in this election cycle supported abortion rights, conservative pro-life Christians were not likely to support them.

And yet Democrats picked up Senate seats in some of the reddest areas of the Bible belt. South Carolina and Texas went Democratic. It seems that even Mississippi – the most churched state in the nation, by some measures – might elect a Democratic senator by the time the final votes are counted. How did that happen?

The answer, I think, has to do partly with the success the Democrats have had in appealing to non-evangelical moderates who might be willing to support a Democrat as long as the Democrats don’t appear to be too secular (or too radical). A couple months before this election, I predicted that progressive Christian Democratic candidates weren’t likely to convert many white evangelicals to their party. I think the exit polls suggest that was probably correct. But even in the Bible belt, there were enough non-evangelical voters to deliver victories to these candidates. And that’s where the second reality I mentioned could continue to help the Democrats a great deal in the future.

2) A politically moderate or progressive Christianity is now politically viable again, and it has the potential to return the Democratic Party to its earlier brand.

From the 1970s through the 2010s, a social justice oriented faith was central to the Democrats’ public image. From 1972 through 1984, every Democratic presidential nominee was either a Methodist minister’s son or (in the case of Jimmy Carter) a Sunday school class teacher and Baptist church deacon. In 1992, the Democratic Party ran two Southern Baptists on a ticket whose slogan was the “new covenant.” In 2008, Democratic presidential nominee Barack Obama talked about his Christian conversion at a Black church in Chicago and he joined his Republican opponent, John McCain, at a “civil forum” at Rick Warren’s Saddleback Church.

The Democratic Party’s connection to progressive Christianity never entirely faded, but in recent years, it was sometimes overshadowed by a secular turn among younger white Democrats, a majority of whom rarely went to church. African American ministers might have a place in Congress as Democratic representatives or senators, but overt expressions of Christianity were much rarer among white Democrats, especially those who were millennials or younger Gen-Xers.

But this week’s midterm elections brought political victories to several Democratic seminarians and ordained white mainline Protestant ministers. James Talarico won in Texas, Adam Hamilton flipped a Senate seat in Kansas, and Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James won House seats in Iowa. Christian faith is back among Democrats – and that’s likely to change the Democratic Party’s public image for the foreseeable future. Perhaps not since the late 1980s have we seen mainline Protestantism and progressive Christianity so well positioned to counter the Religious Right on the public stage.

This means that the political map could once again look a bit like it did in the 1990s, when Democrats (as well as Republicans) were competitive in every region of the country. Republicans could still win Senate victories in New England and the Pacific Northwest, and Democratic presidential candidates still carry several southern states. That was partly because the mainline Protestantism or liberal Catholicism of northern Republicans was still compatible with both the party’s image and the values of the Northeast and Northwest, and because the South still had a lot of voters who were receptive to the message of Southern Baptist moderates like Bill Clinton, Al Gore, and (before that) Jimmy Carter.

We haven’t seen this phenomenon for the past two decades, but this week’s midterm elections restored this political and religious map to a certain extent. Several of the Democrats who won moderately socially conservative red states – most notably, Texas and Kansas – appealed to swing voters in the suburbs by promoting a faith message that was inclusive and pluralistic rather than one that was connected to the culture wars. This was Bill Clinton and Barack Obama’s approach, and Democrats proved on Tuesday that this formula can still win in parts of the South and Midwest.

What does all of this mean for the next election?

Midterm elections cannot tell us which party will win control of the White House in the next election. The “blue wave” of 2006 was followed by a Democratic victory in the presidential election in 2008. But the massive Republican sweep in the 1994 midterm elections did not result in a Republican victory in the next presidential election. Nor did the “red wave” of 2010 produce a GOP presidential triumph in 2012.

But midterm elections can tell us a great deal about the future composition of each party, even if they cannot tell us which party will win in the next election.

For instance, the 1994 “red wave” southernized the Republican Party by replacing a lot of conservative southern Democrats with even more conservative Republicans. That shifted the Republican Party to the right, but it also shifted Democrats to the left, setting the country up for a greater level of partisan polarization for decades to come.

This election did the opposite, I think. By replacing conservative Republican senators and representatives with centrist Democrats in much of the South and Midwest, this election produced a moderating force on the Democratic Party. True, in some areas of the country, centrist Democrats were replaced with more progressive Democrats or even self-proclaimed democratic socialists, but that was counterbalanced with the election of so many centrist Democrats from red states. They’re not at all like the conservative Democrats who used to dominate the South in the 1980s and early 1990s – that is, social conservatives who often opposed abortion and supported gun rights. Instead, they’re pragmatic suburban centrists whose ideological orientation is close to Barack Obama’s – but not necessarily to Zohran Mamdani’s. And in some cases, a progressive Christian faith is a central part of their identity, just as it was for an earlier generation of Democrats.

If that is the case, it means that as the Democrats look toward future elections, they will have a deep bench of young centrists to choose from, and that’s likely to position them for a more geographically diverse appeal than they had in the last presidential election.

But at the same time, the Christian Right is probably also poised to exercise a greater influence on the Republican Party than it did in the last election, because with the erosion of Republican political power in some areas, the Christian Right’s continued loyalty to the Republican Party makes it a potentially more important player in the selection of the next presidential nominee. If some non-evangelical Iowans have abandoned the Republicans for centrist Democrats like Sarah Trone Garriott and Lindsay James, that potentially positions the evangelicals who have remained loyal to the party for an even greater influence in the state’s Republican presidential caucuses.

And Christian Right voters will have no incentive to make peace with religious centrist Democrats, because the views of those Democrats don’t accord with those of white evangelicals on the issues that the Christian Right has traditionally emphasized.

So, the culture wars will likely continue, as will partisan polarization. But this time, the polarization will not fall entirely on lines that suggest a division between a progressive secular party (at least as far as young whites were concerned) and a right-wing religious one. Instead, a center-left Christianity will also play a role in the equation, with a greater number of Democrats now poised to draw on the progressive faith traditions that sustained the party a generation ago.

Daniel K. Williams is an associate professor of history at Ashland University and the author of God’s Own Party: The Making of the Christian Right.
